newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kinkel to visit Turkey to help patch up EU row.
newsitem.headline: Kinkel to visit Turkey to help patch up EU row.

text.p: German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel visits Turkey on Tuesday to try to appease Germany's NATO ally over the European Union's rejection of Ankara's long-standing bid to join the bloc.
Kinkel will meet Turkish Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan and Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller in Ankara on Wednesday and visit Istanbul on Thursday, his ministry said on Monday.

Turkey experts said they expected Kinkel to seek to patch up a bitter row with the EU after the bloc infuriated Turkey by preparing to sign up 11 east European states for membership -- a goal Turkey has cherished in vain for three decades.
"It is certainly not going to be an easy visit. But it is a necessary one," Kinkel told German news magazine Focus.

"Turkey remains on the road to Europe. But there is no doubt it will fail to meet the EU entry requirements for the foreseeable future," Kinkel said, citing "its human rights problems, particularly over the Kurds, and the country's precarious relations with Greece".

Cigdem Akkaya, deputy head of the Centre for Turkish Studies at Germany's Essen University, said Turkish leaders had begun to regard these reasons as a pretext and were convinced the real reason was that Turkey was an Islamic country.
"Turkey has been associated with the EU since 1963 and regards it as unjust that east European states may be admitted while it has been kept out all this time," Akkaya told Reuters.
"(During Kinkel's visit) Turkey will be seeking to show it is not sliding towards fundamentalism and that it draws a clear division between church and state," Akkaya said on Monday.
"I can't imagine the EU will be able to keep Turkey out entirely. They may invite Turkey to join the list of membership candidates to be presented at the EU summit in June," she said.
"But I don't think they will want Turkey in the EU."
Turkey threatened to block NATO's expansion plans in January unless it was granted full EU membership.
"Every NATO state is free to exercise its member rights, but such threats are not clever or helpful," Kinkel said.
Turkey's move prompted Europe's Christian Democrat leaders, including Germany's Chancellor Helmut Kohl, to jointly declare Turkey was unfit for membership because it was an Islamic state.
Kinkel and other EU foreign ministers have distanced themselves from the leaders' position.
The Christian Democrats' reaction also caused serious concern in Washington, which wants to see important NATO ally Turkey close to Europe to stabilise the eastern Mediterranean.
The German minister flies out to Ankara on Tuesday evening from Rome where he is attending anniversary celebrations for the Treaty of Rome, the foreign ministry said in a statement.

He will spend Wednesday in Ankara meeting government officials as well as opposition leader Mesut Yilmaz. He visits Istanbul on Thursday morning and flies to Bulgaria in the afternoon for talks with government officials.
